newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen lower at the open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen lower at the open.

text.p: Wall Street stocks were expected to open lower Monday amid profit-taking and selling pressure on tobacco stocks, analysts said.
But stocks could finish the session higher, boosted by interest in energy and technology stocks following big merger announcements in those sectors, they said.
"We could open lower because we hit new highs on Friday and because of pressures on tobacco stocks," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

The Dow industrials finished up 19 points at a record closing high of 7797 Friday. Shares ended off their peaks after tobacco stocks fell on news of a proposed $368.5 billion settlement between the tobacco industry and the U.S. states.
The Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was down two points at 902.95 this morning, while the long bond was down 3/32 to yield 6.67 percent.

The tobacco accord, announced late Friday afternoon, would require tobacco companies to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate states and smokers for medical treatment and other smoking-related costs.

In the energy sector, Union Pacific Resources Group Inc said it had renewed its attempts to acquire Pennzoil Co after its previous advances were rebuffed. It is now offering a two-step cash and stock deal valued at about $6.4 billion.

"Both energy and computer stocks may fare better as a result of these (merger) announcements," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "The news will provide interest to fuel the stock market."
Japan's Nikkei average closed up 50.60 points at 20,436.14.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that shares of Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJR Nabisco Holdings Inc fell on news of the tobacco accord as some investors took profits and others decided some settlement provisions were too severe.
The New York Times said the tobacco settlement would likely provide plaintiffs' lawyers with the biggest fees in legal history.
